rationale: B wins because it turns the supplied gaps into the story instead of decorating around them. "REI won't say how big its resale business actually is" is a sharper accountability angle than A's unsupported "public retailers can't easily replicate" co-op thesis, which asks an editor to buy a margin argument before the proof exists. A has real bones, but B is cleaner, more skeptical, and more useful to a founder who needs to know what not to pitch yet.
gaps_in_A: "public retailers can't easily replicate" overstates the update. The facts say REI is a member-owned co-op and not publicly traded; they do not prove public retailers lack the same resale-repair options.

"because there are no external shareholders demanding margin protection" is a neat MBA sentence looking for evidence. It may be true as analysis, but the update does not give shareholder pressure, margin, or cannibalization data.
"As outdoor gear floods secondhand apps" imports a market backdrop the prompt never supplied. If you need platform volume data as proof, don't smuggle the conclusion into the headline.

"REI's repair expansion adds skilled technician work" assumes staffing, training, and job classification facts that are not in the update. The proof list catches the hole, but the angle headline has already spent the check.
gaps_in_B: "from a pilot program" is not quite earned. The update says online and select stores, not that REI called it a pilot.
"REI won't say" is sharper than the facts allow. "Not disclosed" is a gap; it is not proof of refusal unless REI was asked and declined.
"they're core retail infrastructure" is a little grand for one retailer's rollout. The angle smartly asks for comparative proof, but the headline gets half a step ahead of the evidence.

The first and fourth angles both ride the same rollout fact: "all 180+ stores" as operations story versus category signal. Keep both only if the founder has data for the category version; otherwise cut the padded twin.
